video_title: The AI Price War Nobody Saw Coming with FirstMark's David Waltcher
gist: FirstMark partner David Waltcher tells Dan Nathan that 2026 is the year companies confront whether 'token maxing' — routing every task to the largest frontier model — is defensible, after open and Chinese models (GLM, MiniMax, Kimi, Qwen) priced around 1/20th per million tokens flipped OpenRouter's closed-versus-open token mix in February 2026. He is 'largely bearish on the application layer' yet argues incumbents like Salesforce are far more durable than public markets assume, sees an unusually rich M&A window (Stripe buying OpenRouter at $7B versus a $1.3B round in May, Silver Lake circling Workday), and has put his last three investments entirely into AI security.

themes.theme: Token maxing and the model price war

insights.claim: FirstMark's David Waltcher predicts 2026 will be the year companies confront whether 'token maxing' — defaulting every task to the largest, most expensive frontier model — is economically defensible, and expects the free market to force routing discipline via labs load-balancing or gateways like OpenRouter.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: If enterprise token spend shifts from 'always frontier' to task-tiered routing, the revenue-per-seat assumptions embedded in frontier-lab valuations and AI-native app pricing need re-underwriting.
insights.quote: I think 2026 will among many things be a year where companies sort of face the truth about whether token maxing is something they want to be doing or not or at least in what capacity.

insights.claim: Waltcher exposes the token-maxing mismatch with a labor analogy: code-generation companies paying 50th-to-60th percentile salaries for engineers are simultaneously paying 100th percentile prices for tokens.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A clean heuristic for spotting AI-native startups with structurally unsustainable COGS — gross margins compress unless they downshift models, so routing adoption becomes a margin catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: Why are they paying 100 percentile for tokens? Why are they using the most expensive biggest and best models for a variety of tasks, some of which actually don't require that level of intelligence?

insights.claim: Waltcher argues the vast majority of a developer's daily tasks — posting a PR, doing code review — do not require the latest Opus-class model, which is why real-time model routing and gateway layers are becoming structurally important.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: The addressable volume for cheap mid-tier and open models is far larger than the frontier-benchmark narrative implies; the routing/gateway layer is the toll booth that captures the spread.
insights.quote: Many of those individual tasks do not require the latest Opus model, right?

insights.claim: Waltcher says that around February 2026 OpenRouter's token mix flipped from roughly 60/40 closed-versus-open to open-model majority as GLM, MiniMax, Kimi and Qwen gained share.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: OpenRouter's public token-share data is a real-time leading indicator of frontier-lab pricing power erosion — a free dataset for tracking the commoditization thesis.
insights.quote: I think it was roughly 60/40 closed open, and it completely flipped. And the open models had this moment.

insights.claim: Waltcher states the open models that took share were priced at roughly one-twentieth the cost per million tokens of closed frontier models while remaining highly performant on everyday tasks.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A 20x price gap at comparable everyday performance is the mechanism behind the price war and caps what frontier labs can charge for undifferentiated workloads.
insights.quote: these models were basically 1/20th of the token cost per million tokens, and they were highly performant at a lot of the things that people do in their every day

insights.claim: Dan Nathan argues Chinese open-source models are directly causing a price war — citing a roughly 70% price cut on the newest flagship model — and warns this creates a serious problem for OpenAI and Anthropic as they ready themselves for IPO.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: If frontier pricing is being set by Chinese open-weight competition rather than capability, pre-IPO revenue quality at the labs is lower than headline growth implies.
insights.quote: So, the Chinese open-source models are causing a price war here.

themes.theme: China's capex asymmetry and the closing model gap

insights.claim: Dan Nathan contrasts Alibaba's three-year capex guidance of $56 billion against roughly $800 billion of combined capex from the four US hyperscalers this year and about $1.5 trillion next year, framing China's AI buildout as radically more capital-efficient.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: If Chinese labs close the capability gap on a low-single-digit percentage of US capex, the hyperscaler capex cycle carries misallocation risk that current semis and power valuations do not price.
insights.quote: Alibaba guided for the next 3 years for CapEx, 56 billion dollars. Our companies, the four hyperscalers, are going to spend 800 billion dollars this year.

insights.claim: Despite the Chinese cost advantage, Waltcher maintains that the most valuable companies in the broader AI universe are American and will remain so for quite some time.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A direct pushback on the 'China wins AI' trade — capability leadership and value accrual can decouple, so cheap Chinese models can pressure pricing without displacing US equity value.
insights.quote: The most valuable companies in the broader AI universe are American-based, and that will be true for I think quite some time.

insights.claim: Nathan frames Microsoft Copilot as the natural distribution channel for cheap models, noting roughly 450 million Office 365 users of whom only about 20 million have converted to Copilot, and that Microsoft has an incentive to bundle rival models to spite OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A roughly 4% Copilot attach rate means Microsoft's cheapest path to conversion is bundling low-cost third-party models — bearish for OpenAI's pricing leverage inside Microsoft's stack.

themes.theme: Application-layer durability vs. the SaaS-is-dead trade

insights.claim: Waltcher holds a two-sided view: he is largely bearish on the application layer overall but believes individual incumbents will prove far more durable than public-market investors assume, producing a haves/have-nots split driven by adaptability, entrenchment and switching costs.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Argues for pair trades within SaaS rather than shorting the group — differentiate on system-of-record status and switching costs instead of applying a blanket AI-disruption discount.
insights.quote: I am I am largely bearish on the application layer. I also think that a lot of these companies are going to be more durable than many in the public market think

insights.claim: Waltcher argues a vibe-coded CRM clone is irrelevant to displacing Salesforce because the real moat is the partner ecosystem, custom implementation channel and decade-plus trust relationships, not the front-end application.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete test for which SaaS names survive AI: score ecosystem and implementation depth, not UI replicability, before pricing in disruption.
insights.quote: whether or not I could vibe code a CRM has actually very little to do with whether I could duplicate that business, right?

insights.claim: Waltcher expects human interaction with systems of record to fall sharply while agentic interaction rises, leaving open whether Salesforce can still command the same contract-size premium — and notes very large AI companies are themselves signing CRM, HRIS and IT help desk contracts today.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Seat-based pricing is the exposed variable, not customer retention — watch net revenue retention and per-contract value at CRM/HRIS/ITSM vendors for the first evidence.

insights.claim: Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter — a company that raised in May at a $1.3 billion valuation and sold for $7 billion — is flagged as the marquee example of AI-era M&A premiums.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A roughly 5x markup within months sets the comp for model-routing and AI-infrastructure assets and shows how aggressively well-capitalized private buyers will pay for strategic positioning.
insights.quote: raised in May at $1.3 billion and it just got bought for $7 billion

insights.claim: Waltcher attributes the current M&A wave to three converging forces: public-market volatility creating cheap assets like Workday (which Silver Lake is circling), previous-era winners such as Stripe buying from a position of strength, and a new class of extremely well-capitalized AI buyers running four or five strategies at once.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A three-factor screen for the next targets: depressed public multiples, plus a strategic gap, plus a buyer with balance-sheet firepower.

insights.claim: Waltcher points to Salesforce's acquisition of Momentum — his first FirstMark investment, which synthesizes live meeting notes into Salesforce — as the template for incumbents buying their way out of the manual data-entry problem as reps shift to using 20 AI tools.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific acquisition thesis for systems of record: buy the agentic capture layer, because the two-hours-a-day manual input behavior that fed the system of record is disappearing.

insights.claim: Waltcher says security has been one of the most active M&A markets for as long as it has existed and that private security transactions close at richer multiples than infrastructure or software counterparts, predicting substantial further consolidation after deals like Google's $32 billion Wiz acquisition.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Security startups carry a structural exit-multiple premium — relevant to venture allocation and to anticipating incumbent buyer behavior post-Wiz.
insights.quote: There's a reason security's been one of the most active M&A markets for as long as it's existed, right?

themes.theme: AI security: agents as the new attack surface

insights.claim: Waltcher says security's entire paradigm has shifted because vulnerability counts have ballooned and effectively everything is becoming a zero day, collapsing the disclosure-to-exploit window to a point traditional security teams cannot defend.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Compressed exploit windows force automation spend regardless of IT budget cycles, making AI security a non-discretionary line item and a defensive growth vector.
insights.quote: the number of vulnerabilities has ballooned. And also just everything's becoming a zero day.

insights.claim: Waltcher has concentrated his last three investments entirely in security — Onyx Security for agent inventory and semantic runtime guardrails, Nebulock for agentic threat hunting, and Tracebit for deception canaries under an 'assumed breach' mindset.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Maps the three emerging AI-security subcategories incumbents are most likely to acquire: agent governance, autonomous threat hunting, and post-breach deception.
insights.quote: my last three investments have all been security investments.

insights.claim: Waltcher frames AI agents as a distinct vulnerability class because they operate stochastically, act far faster than humans, and hold credentials and system access that even the people who provisioned them do not fully understand — the problem Onyx Security addresses at the runtime layer.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Agent inventory and runtime guardrails become a mandatory new CISO budget line — a greenfield category with no incumbent owner yet.

insights.claim: Waltcher cites that roughly 95% of breaches are now credentialed, which he says exposes the failure of the zero-trust paradigm and justifies Tracebit's assumed-breach honeypot approach focused on response speed rather than prevention.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Undermines the investment case for identity-and-authentication-centric security and shifts value toward detection, deception and mean-time-to-respond.
insights.quote: Something like 95% of breaches now are credentialed.

insights.claim: Waltcher expects CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks to be winners of the AI era rather than victims of it, because the breadth of customer resources they already touch converts into an immediate buyer queue for any compelling AI security product.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Distribution and customer trust, not product novelty, determine the winners — supports owning the platform incumbents alongside, not against, the AI-security startup wave.
insights.quote: look at CrowdStrike and Palo. Look at their performance in the public markets.

themes.theme: Market structure, AGI skepticism and downside risks

insights.claim: Waltcher rejects the winner-take-all framing for AI and calls the 'Anthropic wins enterprise, OpenAI wins consumer' split lazy, pointing to OpenAI's Codex numbers as evidence both companies are performing strongly across segments.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Argues against concentrating exposure in a single lab on segment-narrative grounds; momentum rotates with each model and product release.
insights.quote: I even think like comments about Anthropic being the enterprise winner and OpenAI being the consumer winner are a bit lazy.

insights.claim: Waltcher believes the enterprise market is too vast and too vertical-specific for any single lab to capture, citing FirstMark portfolio companies Legora in legal and Nebulock in threat hunting that build proprietary agent harnesses on top of frontier models, analogous to how companies were always built on open source and cloud.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Supports the vertical-AI application thesis at seed and Series A despite platform risk — dependency on a foundation layer has never by itself prevented durable company building.

insights.claim: Waltcher's stated primary derailment risk is macro rather than technological: a major public-market crash or recession would shrink LP public portfolios roughly 30%, making venture look comparatively overweight and stalling new fund commitments with a lag.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: The denominator effect, not an AI capability plateau, is the transmission channel from a public drawdown to a private AI funding freeze — watch LP allocations as the early warning.

insights.claim: Waltcher takes a realist stance on AGI, arguing that even if innovation froze today there would be enormous value left to create because adoption is very early across industries and geographies, and that continued improvement in cost, speed, performance and capability alone sustains the supercycle.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Decouples the AI investment case from AGI timelines and gives four concrete trajectory variables as the real invalidation test, hedging against lab leaders repeatedly pushing out grandiose milestones.
insights.quote: I think if the world froze today from an innovation standpoint there would be so much value still to be created in AI.
